_comment: The commodity board. Edit freely; the server re-reads this file on every rebuild. Each entry: id, label, group, unit (display only), sources (yahoo = daily history + live level from Yahoo's keyless chart API; te = Trading Economics summary sentence, level plus day/month/year change only, no chart; fred = monthly IMF/World Bank history from FRED, two to three months behind, used for the long chart and the vs-peak read when Yahoo has no contract). cost = industries that BUY this commodity (a rise squeezes their margin); revenue = industries that SELL it or own the resource (a rise helps them). These two lists are the universal, geography-free layer of the exposure map. The names behind each industry live in exposure_<market>.json per market so the same board works in any country. Pass-through notes are general: a specific company's raw-material share and pricing power come from its own filings, never from here. fred_unit is the unit of the FRED series (IMF units differ from the exchange contract), shown only when FRED is the level on screen.

commodities.label: WTI crude
commodities.note: Airlines pass it through with a lag of one to two quarters via fares; refiners care about the crack spread, not the level.

commodities.label: Brent crude
commodities.note: The import benchmark for India and Asia. A sustained move shows up in the current-account and the currency before it shows up in any income statement.

commodities.label: Nat gas (Henry Hub)
commodities.note: US nitrogen fertiliser makers are the most direct cost play; US gas is cheap versus Europe and Asia, so the spread matters more than the level.

commodities.label: EU gas (TTF)
commodities.note: The energy-intensity gap between Europe and the US is the whole story for European heavy industry margins.

commodities.label: Gasoline (RBOB)
commodities.note: A consumer-wallet read more than an industrial input; a rise taxes discretionary spend.

commodities.label: Thermal coal (Newcastle)
commodities.note: In India the domestic e-auction price and Coal India's notified price move far less than the seaborne benchmark; the seaborne number hits importers and the merchant power tariff.

commodities.label: Uranium (U3O8)
cost: Nuclear utilities (fuel, small share of cost)
commodities.note: Fuel is a small share of a nuclear plant's cost, so the price barely touches utilities; it is a pure miner and enricher story.

commodities.label: Copper
commodities.note: Cable makers usually pass it through on a formula with a one-quarter lag; the risk is inventory revaluation on a sharp reversal.

commodities.label: Aluminium
commodities.note: Smelters are a power-cost story as much as a metal-price story; check captive power before the LME price.

commodities.label: Zinc
commodities.note: Galvanising is the dominant use, so zinc rides construction and auto volumes.

commodities.label: Nickel
commodities.note: Stainless is the bigger buyer; the battery narrative moves the price more than the tonnage justifies.

commodities.label: Lead
commodities.note: Battery makers price on a formula, so the cost is passed on within a quarter unless competition breaks the formula.

commodities.label: Tin
commodities.note: Solder is a tiny share of an electronics bill of materials; the price matters to miners, not to buyers.

commodities.label: Iron ore (62% Fe)
commodities.note: Who owns the mine decides the sign: an integrated steel maker with captive ore is a beneficiary, a converter without one is squeezed.

commodities.label: Steel (China HRC)
commodities.note: China sets the marginal price for Asia; Indian steel prices trade at a premium set by import parity and duties, so check the landed price, not only Shanghai.

commodities.label: Lithium carbonate
commodities.note: Cell makers pass most of it through on indexed contracts; the EV maker with a fixed-price sales list eats the residual.

commodities.label: Cobalt
commodities.note: Supply is Congo policy; a price spike is usually an export decision, not demand.

commodities.label: Gold
revenue: Gold loan lenders (LTV cushion, a rise helps)
commodities.note: Miners are levered to the price through fixed costs; a jeweller's margin is on making charges, so a rise mostly hurts volumes and helps inventory value.

commodities.label: Silver
commodities.note: Half industrial, half monetary; solar paste demand is the marginal industrial buyer.

commodities.label: Platinum
commodities.note: Diesel share of autos drives it; the electrolyser story is future demand, not present.

commodities.label: Palladium
commodities.note: Pure petrol-car catalyst metal; EV penetration is the structural bear case.

commodities.label: Wheat (CBOT)
commodities.note: Packaged-food makers pass it through with a two-quarter lag and usually keep the price when wheat falls back.

commodities.label: Corn
commodities.note: Feed is the biggest use; poultry margins move inversely with corn and soymeal.

commodities.label: Soybeans
commodities.note: Crushers earn the spread between beans and meal plus oil; the level matters less than the crush margin.

commodities.label: Soybean oil
commodities.note: Competes with palm oil; the palm-soy spread decides which importer switches.

commodities.label: Palm oil (Malaysia)
commodities.note: The largest edible oil import for India; consumer-staples margins in India move with it, with a one-quarter lag.

commodities.label: Rough rice
commodities.note: Export policy moves it more than weather; India's export bans and duties are the swing factor.

commodities.label: Sugar (No. 11)
commodities.note: Indian mills sell at a government-set minimum, so the world price matters to them mainly through export quotas.

commodities.label: Coffee (Arabica)
revenue: Instant coffee exporters (cost-plus, volume not price)
commodities.note: Cafes hedge a year out, so a spike hits their P&L two to four quarters later.

commodities.label: Cocoa
commodities.note: Confectioners shrink the bar before they raise the price; watch volume, not just gross margin.

commodities.label: Cotton
commodities.note: Spinners carry three to six months of inventory; a fall after a spike is the dangerous leg because they are stuck with expensive cotton.

commodities.label: Lumber
commodities.note: A US housing-starts proxy; homebuilders pass it through only in a strong market.

commodities.label: Natural rubber
commodities.note: Rubber is the largest single raw material for a tyre maker; the hit lands one to two quarters later, and only the maker with pricing power recovers it. The India domestic grade (RSS4) and the global benchmark can diverge for months.

commodities.label: Synthetic rubber
commodities.note: Tracks butadiene and therefore crude; when natural and synthetic rise together the tyre maker has no substitution escape.

commodities.label: Urea
cost: Fertiliser makers on imported gas (margin is the subsidy formula)
revenue: Urea producers (gas-advantaged: Middle East, US, Russia)
commodities.note: In India the farmer price is fixed, so a rise in world urea is a fiscal subsidy cost, not a company cost; the producer with cheap gas wins.

commodities.label: Polypropylene
commodities.note: Converters pass it through monthly on a formula; the margin risk is a sharp reversal on inventory.

commodities.label: Methanol
commodities.note: A coal and gas derivative; China's MTO plants set the marginal demand.

commodities.label: Naphtha
commodities.note: The Asian cracker feedstock; a naphtha spike with flat polymer prices is a direct margin squeeze on non-integrated chemical makers.

commodities.label: Ethanol
commodities.note: In India the blending price is administered; the world price matters to exporters and to the corn-versus-sugar feedstock choice.

commodities.label: Baltic Dry Index
commodities.note: A demand-for-raw-materials read: iron ore, coal and grain tonnage. It leads industrial commodity prices by weeks when the move is real.

commodities.label: Heating oil (diesel proxy)
commodities.note: Diesel and jet fuel price off this distillate crack, not off crude alone; a wide crack with flat crude is a refiner's quarter and a trucker's problem.

commodities.label: EU carbon permits
cost: Exporters to the EU under CBAM (steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser)
commodities.note: From 2026 the EU's border levy (CBAM) prices this into Indian steel and aluminium exports to Europe; the permit price is the levy rate.

commodities.label: Coking coal (Australia)
commodities.note: The single largest imported input for Indian blast-furnace steel; India imports most of its metallurgical coal, mainly from Australia. Lands in steel cost with a one-quarter lag through inventory.

commodities.label: Steel (US Midwest HRC)
commodities.note: The tariff-protected US price; the gap to China HRC is the tariff wall and the export opportunity for everyone outside it.

commodities.label: Tea (India auction)
commodities.note: An Indian auction price in rupees; packaged brands pass it through slowly and estates take it at once.

commodities.label: Sunflower oil
commodities.note: India's second imported edible oil after palm; Black Sea supply sets it. The palm-sunflower spread decides which one the Indian refiner buys.

commodities.label: Soybean meal
commodities.note: Feed is two-thirds of a poultry producer's cost and soymeal is the protein half of feed; corn is the other half.

commodities.label: Bitumen
commodities.note: Road contracts in India carry a price-variation clause that lags by a quarter or more; the contractor eats the gap.

commodities.label: Kraft pulp
revenue: Integrated paper makers with own pulp
commodities.note: Who owns the pulp mill decides the sign, same as iron ore for steel.

commodities.label: USD/INR
cost: Importers of dollar-priced inputs (every commodity above, in rupee terms)
commodities.note: A rise here is a weaker rupee. It multiplies every dollar commodity on this board for an Indian buyer, so a flat crude price with a 5% weaker rupee is a 5% fuel-cost rise.

commodities.label: USD/CNY
cost: Indian makers competing with Chinese imports (steel, chemicals, solar modules, electronics)
commodities.note: A rise is a weaker yuan, which makes Chinese steel, chemicals and modules cheaper on Indian shores; the China-priced cards above (steel, lithium, polypropylene, methanol) read in this currency.
